title: When the Visitor Wakes
premise: Wren Marchetti, a pest controller in the dying town of Hollow Creek, is hired to clear an infestation at the old Vesper house — but the 'pests' leave fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. When Wren sets up sleep recordings to monitor the property's last resident, the tapes capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, a voice that knows Wren's name and their dead mother's lullaby. The voice belongs to the Visitor, an entity sustained by sung inheritance: each generation of Vespers must learn its song to keep it sleeping, and the last heir is dying without passing it on. Drawn into the house by dreams they cannot refuse, Wren discovers they are the illegitimate bloodline the family hid — the only one left who can carry the verse. In the climax, Wren must sing the final verse back to the Visitor without surrendering their own voice to it, choosing love for the dying heir Odile over the duty of becoming the next keeper; they break the cycle by teaching the song to no one, letting the Visitor wake briefly, starve, and dissolve — but the price is Wren's memory of every lullaby they ever loved.
about_author: Felix Lockridge is the pen name of a former night-shift security guard who spent six years listening to empty buildings through cheap microphones. They write horror about houses that keep records, and live alone with a dog who barks at the hallway.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Inside
chapters.summary: Wren Marchetti takes a routine pest-control call at the derelict Vesper house and finds greasy handprints pressed against the inside of boarded windows — prints too large for any animal, arranged like someone waving goodbye. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: professional skepticism curdling into unease as the town's silence about the house becomes louder than any explanation.

chapters.title: The Client Who Counts Doors
chapters.summary: Wren meets Odile Vesper, the house's last living heir, a gaunt woman in her seventies who pays double but insists Wren count the doors aloud on entering and leaving. There are eleven doors; there should be ten. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: reluctant tenderness toward a client who is clearly more afraid of her own home than of dying.

chapters.title: Bait Stations and Bad Air
chapters.summary: Wren lays traps through the house's lower floors, noticing dust undisturbed for decades except along one worn path from the cellar to Odile's bedroom. The air tastes faintly of copper and hymnals. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the creeping realization that this isn't an infestation — something here is being fed on purpose.

chapters.title: Recording the Dark
chapters.summary: At Odile's request, Wren installs audio recorders to capture whatever moves at night, and Odile makes them promise never to play the tapes during daylight hours. That first night, Wren sleeps badly and wakes humming a tune they don't recognize. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: dread arriving sideways, through the body before the mind.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Playing the night's recording after midnight, Wren hears Odile talking in her sleep — and a second voice, wet and patient, answering questions she never asked aloud. It asks about children. It asks about bloodlines. Then it says Wren's name. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: terror sharpening into obsession; Wren plays the tape four more times.

chapters.title: Hollow Creek Remembers Nothing
chapters.summary: Wren digs into county records and finds the Vesper genealogy suspiciously clean — daughters unlisted, marriages erased, one line struck through in different ink. The town librarian goes pale when shown the house's address and refuses to speak above a whisper. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; the whole town has agreed not to know.

chapters.title: What Odile Keeps Under Lock
chapters.summary: Odile catches Wren snooping and, instead of anger, shows them a hymnal bound in grey leather, its final page holding half a verse written in a child's handwriting. She calls it 'the keeping-song' and warns: learn it wrong and you'll sing along forever. POV: alternating Wren and Odile. Emotional beat: guarded trust forming between two people out of options.

chapters.title: The Dream With Questions
chapters.summary: Wren dreams of standing in the Vesper cellar while something behind the walls asks them questions in their mother's voice — questions about whether they were loved, whether they were wanted. They wake with dirt under their fingernails. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: grief weaponized; the entity has found the softest door.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors Again
chapters.summary: During a routine visit, Wren counts twelve doors. The new one stands where a wall used to be, warm to the touch, breathing faintly. Odile sees it and begins packing a bag, then unpacks it, weeping — she cannot leave; leaving means it follows. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the horror stops being containable; the house is growing toward them.

chapters.title: The Verse Half-Learned
chapters.summary: Odile teaches Wren the first lines of the keeping-song, explaining the covenant: the Vespers have sung the Visitor asleep for two hundred years, and she is the last singer. Her diagnosis gives her months. Wren refuses the inheritance outright and walks out. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: heartbreak of a keeper watching her duty die with her.

chapters.title: Tapes From Before
chapters.summary: Wren finds older recordings hidden in the attic — decades of them — each capturing a different Vesper singing to the dark, each ending mid-verse when the singer's voice simply stops. On the oldest tape, a young woman's voice sings a melody Wren's mother used to hum. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the past reaching up and claiming kinship.

chapters.title: Mother's Lullaby, Wrong Key
chapters.summary: Wren confronts their aunt, the family's last honest liar, and learns the truth: Wren's mother was a Vesper daughter, erased from the record, fled rather than sing. She didn't escape it — she just delayed it, and it learned Wren's name from her deathbed. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: fury and recognition braided together; the inheritance was always theirs.

chapters.title: It Starts Answering Back
chapters.summary: The Visitor begins speaking to Wren while they're awake — through faucets, through static, once through a customer's car radio. It is courteous, even kind, offering to return their mother's voice if they'll only come and finish learning the song. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: seduction; the horror's most dangerous face is generosity.

chapters.title: Odile Fails the Verse
chapters.summary: Racing her illness, Odile attempts the full keeping-song alone and falters on the penultimate line. That night the house exhales; frost blooms indoors in July; the eleventh door opens onto a stairway going down into warmth. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: failure and shame — she has weakened the seal her ancestors died maintaining.

chapters.title: The Town That Sold Its Silence
chapters.summary: Wren learns why Hollow Creek stays quiet: generations ago the town traded its memory of the bargain for safety, letting the Vespers carry it alone. Now neighbors begin dreaming the Visitor's questions, and three families quietly pack their cars. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: righteous anger at complicity, and the loneliness of being the only one who remembers.

chapters.title: Terms of Inheritance
chapters.summary: The Visitor offers Wren a bargain directly: sing the last verse as its new keeper and it will spare Odile a painful death, restore Wren's mother's voice, keep everyone safe forever. Duty dressed as mercy. Wren, exhausted and grieving, almost says yes. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh — survival offered at the exact price of everything worth surviving for.

chapters.title: Love Against the Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile, lucid for one clear evening, tells Wren the covenant's secret flaw: the song requires a willing heir, and willingness can be refused. She begs Wren not to take it — not for safety, but because she watched her own mother become the thing's instrument and lost her entirely. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: a dying woman spending her last strength to free someone else.

chapters.title: Descent Through the Twelfth Door
chapters.summary: The Visitor, tired of patience, takes Odile down the stairway behind the twelfth door to force the transfer. Wren follows with the grey hymnal, a recorder running, and every light they can carry, counting doors aloud like a prayer. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into resolve; going down anyway.

chapters.title: The Song's Last Verse
chapters.summary: In the cellar-heart of the house, Wren finds Odile held inside a sound like a held breath, and the Visitor wearing the assembled voices of every keeper before her. To save Odile, Wren must complete the verse — so they sing it backward, returning it, note by note, refusing to keep it. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the climax; love deployed as refusal, the song given back instead of handed down.

chapters.title: What Wakes Must Starve
chapters.summary: Unfinished and unowned, the Visitor wakes fully for the first time in two centuries — and finds nothing left to feed it, because no one will inherit the hunger. It unravels through the house, taking the doors with it, screaming in every voice it ever borrowed, including, briefly, Wren's mother's. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: awful triumph; victory that sounds like mourning.

chapters.title: The Price of Quiet
chapters.summary: Odile dies peacefully a week later, the house ordinary around her, eleven doors where ten should be and no one able to say why. Wren realizes the breaking took its toll: every lullaby they've ever loved is gone from memory — their mother's voice among them. They hum nothing, and the silence holds. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: grief and release entangled; survival paid in full.

chapters.title: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: Months later, Wren keeps the pest-control route through Hollow Creek, checks on the emptied Vesper house, and teaches nothing to anyone. A young caller asks about strange noises in her walls, and Wren goes — lights on, doors counted, recorder off. Some songs are better left unsung, and some inheritances better buried. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: hard-won peace, vigilance chosen freely at last.
